title: Should a client outsource the work or keep it in-house?
description: Outsource or keep in-house? for case interviews. Make-or-buy questions in operations and cost cases. A checklist, a worked example and how to say it.
hook: A client should outsource when an outside provider can do the work more cheaply or flexibly at acceptable quality, and the work is not a source of its advantage; it should keep the work in-house when control, quality or know-how matter more than the saving. Decide on total cost, including transition and management, and on the outcome for customers, not on the vendor's headline price.
body:
When it helps

Make-or-buy questions come up in cost reduction and operations cases: should the client run its own call centre, warehouse, IT or parts production, or pay someone else to?

The comparison

ForAgainst
OutsourceLower cost; focus on the core; less risk if volumes fallLess control over quality; reliance on others; brand risk
Keep in-houseControl over process and quality; keeps know-howHigher fixed costs; capacity tied up

An example: a bank's call centre

A bank is thinking of outsourcing its customer call centre. For: lower cost per call, and easier to scale up and down. Against: customers may notice worse service, and the bank loses direct sight of what customers complain about. A sensible middle way is often to outsource simple calls and keep complex or high-value ones in-house.

Build the full business case

An illustrative online retailer handles 200,000 customer enquiries a year.

  • In-house, the fully loaded cost is $7 an enquiry: 200,000 × $7 = $1.4M a year.
  • A vendor quotes $5.25 an enquiry: 200,000 × $5.25 = $1.05M a year.
  • Headline saving: $350,000 a year.

That is not yet the business case. Add the costs of outsourcing: staff to manage the vendor, technology links and any minimum-volume commitment. Suppose they add $150,000 a year, plus $250,000 once to make the transition.

  • Recurring saving: $350,000 − $150,000 = $200,000 a year.
  • Payback on the transition: $250,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.25 years.

Now test service. If each customer is worth $50 a year in contribution, losing 4,000 customers to slower or worse responses ($200,000 ÷ $50) wipes out the whole saving. So the contract needs clear service targets, and a split may beat all-or-nothing: outsource order-status questions, and keep complex refunds and vulnerable customers in-house.

How it sounds in an interview

"The vendor saves $350,000 on paper, but after managing it we keep about $200,000 a year, with a payback of just over a year. That saving disappears if we lose more than about 4,000 customers, so I'd outsource the simple enquiries first, with service targets, and keep the complex ones."

The weak version compares hourly wages, says "outsourcing is cheaper" and stops.

Common mistakes

  • Using the vendor's price as the saving, without transition and management costs.
  • Ignoring the effect on customers and on know-how.
  • Treating it as all-or-nothing when the work can be split.

Practise it

1. A firm's 30-person payroll team costs $1.35M a year. A provider quotes $1.1M. The firm would keep one manager at $70,000 to oversee it, and the switch costs $150,000. What is the annual saving and the payback?

Show the answer

Saving: $1.35M − $1.1M − $70,000 = $180,000 a year. Payback: $150,000 ÷ $180,000 ≈ 0.8 years, about ten months. Payroll is rarely a source of advantage, so this looks attractive if accuracy can be guaranteed in the contract.

2. Should a premium car maker outsource the design of its engines?

Show the answer

Probably not. Engine design is likely part of what customers pay a premium for, and outsourcing it would hand know-how to a supplier who could also serve rivals. It might outsource standard parts instead.

Where to practise next

Try Marble Auto Parts (outsource a part to save money, or to free the factory?) or Heatherfield Hotels (should a hotel group run its own laundry?).
